analysis.one_liner: Sets federal health and safety standards for teen residential treatment programs and lets families sue over abuse.
analysis.headline: The bill had 28 House sponsors including one Republican, but the House Education and the Workforce Committee never acted on it before the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required residential programs for teens — wilderness expeditions, boot camps, therapeutic boarding schools, and behavior-modification facilities — to meet minimum federal standards banning abuse, extreme seclusion and restraints, and discipline that withholds food, water, or medical care. It would have required staff criminal background checks, licensed clinicians on site, phone access for kids, and detailed disclosures to parents about deaths, prior violations, and staff qualifications. It also created civil penalties of up to $50,000 per violation, a private right of action for injured families, and a Justice Department enforcement backstop.
analysis.who_benefits: Children placed in residential treatment and behavior-modification programs, and their parents, who would gain enforceable safety standards, required staff screening and training, guaranteed contact with their kids, and the right to sue for injuries.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Teens in residential programs and their parents

how_it_helps.text: Bans child abuse and neglect, punishment that withholds essential food, water, clothing, shelter, or medical care, and treatment designed to humiliate or degrade a child, and bars seclusion and restraints that impair breathing or communication except in narrow emergencies.

Requires every staff member and volunteer to pass criminal history and sex-offender registry checks and be trained to recognize and report abuse, suicide risk, and medical emergencies, and requires a licensed clinician on site at all times.

Guarantees children reasonable access to a phone, written correspondence, and abuse hotline numbers, and requires programs to notify parents within six hours of any abuse investigation or health and safety violation.

Requires programs to disclose to parents, in writing, staff qualifications, prior violations and penalties, the number of children who left before completing the program, and the number and causes of deaths over the past ten years, and creates a private right of action for anyone injured by a violation.

Directs HHS to oversee and investigate reports of abuse, impose civil penalties up to $50,000 per violation, refer unremedied violations to the Attorney General, and raises state child-abuse-prevention grant funding to $200 million per year with conditions that states license and inspect covered programs.

analysis.who_pays: The residential treatment industry, which would bear compliance costs, penalties of up to $50,000 per violation, and liability from the new right to sue, costs that would partly flow through to parents in program fees; plus federal appropriations of $5 million per year and expanded state child-abuse grant funding.
analysis.who_pays_short: Residential teen program operators and taxpayers

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs, liability exposure, and penalties could push smaller programs out of business, reducing options for parents of children with severe behavioral or mental health needs who feel they have nowhere else to turn.

The bill authorizes $200 million per year in state grant funding and $5 million per year for HHS oversight but appropriations would still be required each year, so the enforcement scheme could be underfunded in practice.
Federal minimum standards and a federal private right of action would overlay the state licensing regimes some states already run, raising questions about duplicative oversight.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — enforceable bans on abuse, starvation discipline, suffocating restraints, and isolation of children in programs marketed to desperate parents — is substantial, and the disclosure and background-check requirements address documented harms. The honest costs are compliance burdens on small operators and the possibility that some programs close, but given that the bill's baseline concern is children dying or being abused in unregulated facilities, the trade-off weighs clearly on the side of the standards.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee and then to a subcommittee, and no markup or vote ever happened before the 114th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Adam Schiff introduced the bill on July 14, 2015, with 12 original cosponsors including Republican Rep. Ileana Ros-Lehtinen.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce on the day it was introduced.
On November 16, 2015, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Early Childhood, Elementary, and Secondary Education, and no further action was recorded for the remainder of the Congress.
The bill finished with 27 cosponsors, 26 Democrats and 1 Republican, but the committee never reported it and the House never voted on it before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Residential teen treatment and behavior-modification operators kept operating without federal safety standards, staff screening requirements, mandatory disclosure of deaths and violations, or exposure to the $50,000-per-violation penalties and lawsuits the bill would have allowed. Families with children in these programs gained nothing.

industries.industry: Residential teen treatment industry (behavior-modification programs, wilderness therapy, boot camps, therapeutic boarding schools)
industries.note: These programs charge parents tens of thousands of dollars to house and treat their children with little outside oversight. The bill would have imposed federal safety standards, mandatory background checks, disclosure of deaths and prior violations, penalties up to $50,000 per violation, and a right to sue, so the industry's interest in avoiding oversight ran directly against child safety.

industries.industry: State child protection and licensing agencies
industries.note: The bill would have conditioned federal child-abuse-prevention grants on states licensing, inspecting, and reporting on covered residential programs, with funding raised to $200 million per year.
